newsitem.title: USA: More banks boost prime lending rates. [CORRECTED 17:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: More banks boost prime lending rates. [CORRECTED 17:30 GMT]

text.p: Chase Manhattan, the nation's largest bank, Wednesday joined the parade of institutions boosting their lending rates, one day after the Federal Reserve raised a key short-term interest rate for the first time since 1995 (corrects from 1994).
Chase Manhattan said it was raising its prime lending rate to 8.50 percent from 8.25 percent, effective immediately.
The prime rate is linked to many types of consumer loans, including credit cards, adjustable mortgages and home equity loans.
Bankers Trust, J.P. Morgan & Co., PNC Bank NA, First Chicago NBD Corp., NationsBank Corp. and Mellon Bank all said they were raising their prime rates to 8.50 percent.

On Tuesday, Columbus, Ohio-based Banc One, the nation's 10th-largest bank, was the first to boost its prime rate. It was followed by Citibank, a unit of Citicorp, and Central Fidelity Banks Inc. of Richmond, Va.

After a meeting Tuesday of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee, the central bank announced an increase of 25 basis points in the federal funds rate, saying it viewed the action as a "prudent step that affords greater assurance of prolonging the current economic expansion by sustaining the existing low inflation environment through the rest of this year and next."
The federal funds rate is the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans.
The last time the central bank tightened monetary policy was on Feb. 1, 1995.
